definition: Tome means a large, heavy book.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word tome. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know tome should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Somewhere in every law office lobby sits a leather tome no one has opened since the firm bought it by the yard.
A booklet is the featherweight end of the line — stapled pages you read standing up and forget in a coat pocket, as far from a tome as print gets.
A textbook stops short of a tome — a schoolbag staple, heavy enough to notice on your shoulder, while a tome is heft you plan a whole shelf around.

A volume is any single bound book, big or small — the librarian's neutral counting word, as happy with a slim yearbook as with a monster. Tome refuses to be neutral: it insists on size and heft. Every tome is a volume; only the back-straining ones are tomes.

Doorstop is the joke name for a book this size — pure teasing, with the affection optional. Tome carries the same wink more gently: it respects the book's weight even while smiling at it. Call a dictionary a tome and you admire it; call it a doorstop and you're done reading.

An opus is a creator's major work, measured in importance rather than pounds — a symphony can be an opus and weigh nothing at all. A tome is measured at the shelf: physical size and heft, whatever the contents amount to. Opus praises the achievement; tome weighs the object.

Apprentices roll it out on a cart built for the purpose and are forbidden, by long tradition, to move it alone.
Tome is the word because it means a large, heavy book — the size is the point, and affection and mockery ride along with it.

For her raptor project, Jun requested the library's copy of Birds of the Northern Hemisphere and discovered it could not be checked out — partly because it was reference, mostly because it was a tome.
Eleven pounds, one thousand four hundred pages, a spine as wide as her forearm.
The librarian wheeled it to her table on a cart.
Jun spent four afternoons with it and came to love the heft: every hawk she could name had six pages, three plates, and a range map.
Her notebook, by contrast, weighed nothing and held everything she was allowed to take home.
